gloss: A craftsman who shapes molten glass by blowing air into it through a tube.
examples: We watched a *glassblower* shape a vase in about ten minutes.
The museum has a studio where *glassblowers* work every afternoon.
Her uncle was a *glassblower* in Ohio for forty years.

gloss: An eye disease in which pressure inside the eye slowly damages vision.
examples: My grandmother is being treated for *glaucoma*.
*Glaucoma* often has no symptoms in the early stages.
The eye doctor checks for *glaucoma* at every visit.

gloss: A faint or brief light, or a bright reflection from a smooth surface.
examples: There was a *gleam* of light under the door.
I saw a *gleam* of amusement in his eyes.
The polished floor gave off soft *gleams*.

gloss: A quick, incomplete look at something.
examples: I caught a *glimpse* of her in the crowd.
The book gives us a *glimpse* of life in the 1930s.
We only got *glimpses* of the ocean through the trees.

gloss: A small, quick flash of light reflected off something.
examples: A *glint* of gold showed under the dirt.
There was a *glint* of metal in the tall grass.
The lake threw off *glints* of afternoon sun.

gloss: Someone who travels to many different countries.
examples: My aunt is a real *globetrotter*.
The magazine is written for *globetrotters* on a budget.
After he retired, he turned into a *globetrotter*.

gloss: Near darkness, or a heavy feeling of sadness and hopelessness.
examples: We could barely see each other in the *gloom*.
A mood of *gloom* settled over the office after the layoffs.
The news did nothing to lift the *gloom*.

gloss: Great fame and honor won by an achievement, or magnificent beauty.
examples: The team came home covered in *glory*.
He wanted the money, not the *glory*.
In October the canyon is in its full *glory*.

gloss: A simple sugar that the body uses as its main source of energy.
examples: Diabetics have to watch their blood *glucose*.
The nurse checked her *glucose* level before breakfast.
Fruit juice is high in *glucose*.

gloss: A supply of something that is far larger than what is needed.
examples: A *glut* of oil pushed prices down.
There's a *glut* of apartments on the market this spring.
Warm weather produced a *glut* of tomatoes.

gloss: A salt of glutamic acid, used in cooking as a flavor enhancer and present naturally in some foods.
examples: The label says the soup contains monosodium *glutamate*.
Some people claim *glutamate* gives them headaches.
*Glutamate* occurs naturally in tomatoes and aged cheese.

gloss: A protein found in wheat and some other grains.
examples: She can't eat *gluten*.
This bread is made without *gluten*.
*Gluten* is what makes dough stretchy.

gloss: Someone who eats far too much, or who is unusually eager for something.
examples: He's a *glutton* at every holiday dinner.
She's a *glutton* for punishment — she signed up for another marathon.
The old history calls the emperor a drunk and a *glutton*.

gloss: The habit of eating and drinking far more than you need.
examples: Thanksgiving is an open invitation to *gluttony*.
The sermon warned against *gluttony* and greed.
He looks back on those years of *gluttony* with some regret.

gloss: Small Italian dumplings made from potato or flour and boiled.
examples: We ordered *gnocchi* with sage butter.
She makes *gnocchi* from scratch every Sunday.
The *gnocchi* here is better than the pasta.
contrast: The g is silent and cch is a k sound: NYAH-kee.

gloss: A small imaginary creature like a little bearded old man, often made as a garden statue.
examples: There's a plastic *gnome* by the front steps.
The story is full of dwarves and *gnomes*.
Someone stole two *gnomes* from her flower bed.

gloss: A large African antelope with a heavy head and curved horns.
examples: A herd of *gnus* crossed the river.
The documentary followed the *gnu* migration.
We saw zebras, giraffes, and a single *gnu*.
contrast: The g is silent: NOO. Americans usually call this animal a wildebeest.

gloss: An ugly, mischievous creature in folklore and fantasy stories.
examples: The kids dressed as *goblins* for Halloween.
In the movie, a *goblin* guards the gate.
She told them a story about a *goblin* in the woods.

gloss: A child that an adult promises at a baptism to help raise.
examples: She sends her *godchild* a card every birthday.
He has four *godchildren* now.
My *godchild* just turned ten.

gloss: A girl that an adult promises at a baptism to help raise.
examples: My *goddaughter* is starting college this fall.
He took his *goddaughter* to the zoo on Saturday.
Both of her *goddaughters* live in Texas.

gloss: A boy that an adult promises at a baptism to help raise.
examples: His *godson* is named after him.
She flew out to watch her *godson* graduate.
He bought bikes for both of his *godsons*.

gloss: A swelling in the neck caused by an enlarged thyroid gland.
examples: Iodized salt nearly eliminated *goiter* in the United States.
The doctor noticed a small *goiter* during the exam.
*Goiters* were common in regions with little iodine in the diet.

gloss: A tall wild plant with clusters of small yellow flowers that bloom in late summer.
examples: The field was thick with *goldenrod*.
*Goldenrod* blooms along the highway every September.
Bees crowded the *goldenrods* by the fence.

gloss: A craftsman who makes objects and jewelry out of gold.
examples: The ring was made by a local *goldsmith*.
Her father trained as a *goldsmith* in Italy.
Medieval *goldsmiths* often worked as bankers too.

gloss: A long, narrow Venetian boat, or an enclosed cabin hanging from a cable.
examples: We took a *gondola* through the canals.
The ski *gondola* runs until four o'clock.
Six *gondolas* were tied up along the water.

gloss: A large metal disk that makes a deep ringing sound when it is struck.
examples: A *gong* announced that dinner was ready.
He hit the *gong* twice and the room went quiet.
The temple had two bronze *gongs*.

gloss: A sexually transmitted infection caused by bacteria.
examples: *Gonorrhea* can usually be treated with antibiotics.
The clinic tests for *gonorrhea* and chlamydia.
Cases of *gonorrhea* have risen for the third year in a row.

gloss: Benefit or advantage, especially to people in general.
examples: She did it for the *good* of the whole town.
What *good* will complaining do?
The rest did him a lot of *good*.
contrast: The plural goods means merchandise (товары), not benefits.

gloss: A small, sour green berry that grows on a thorny bush.
examples: She made a pie out of *gooseberries*.
There's a *gooseberry* bush behind the shed.
The *gooseberries* aren't ripe yet.

gloss: A small burrowing rodent that digs tunnels and leaves mounds of dirt.
examples: A *gopher* has been tearing up the lawn.
The field was full of *gopher* holes.
*Gophers* carry food in their cheek pouches.

gloss: Blood from a wound, especially the bloodshed shown in violent movies.
examples: The movie has too much *gore* for me.
There's plenty of suspense but very little *gore*.
He describes the battle without dwelling on the *gore*.

gloss: A strong Italian blue cheese.
examples: The salad comes with walnuts and *gorgonzola*.
He melted *gorgonzola* over the steak.
I bought a wedge of *gorgonzola* at the deli.

gloss: A person who follows a dark style of rock music and dresses mostly in black.
examples: She was a *goth* in high school.
A few *goths* were hanging around outside the club.
He still dresses like a *goth* at forty.

gloss: A mild yellow Dutch cheese.
examples: I put smoked *gouda* on the sandwich.
A wheel of *gouda* sat on the counter.
*Gouda* melts nicely on a burger.

gloss: A groove or hole cut or scraped into a surface.
examples: The movers left a *gouge* in the hardwood floor.
There were deep *gouges* in the tree bark.
He filled the *gouge* with wood putty.

gloss: A thick Hungarian stew of meat and vegetables seasoned with paprika.
examples: She made *goulash* for dinner.
The *goulash* was thick with beef and onions.
He orders *goulash* every time we go there.

gloss: A hard-skinned fruit related to the pumpkin, often dried for decoration or used as a container.
examples: She arranged *gourds* on the table for Thanksgiving.
The birdhouse was made from a dried *gourd*.
We grew a *gourd* the size of a football.

gloss: A painful disease that makes joints, often the big toe, swell up.
examples: His *gout* flares up after a rich meal.
*Gout* runs in the family.
She takes medication for *gout* every day.

gloss: A woman employed to teach and care for children in a private home.
examples: The children were raised by a *governess*.
In the novel she works as a *governess* in a country house.
Two *governesses* lived on the top floor.

gloss: The position or term of office of a governor.
examples: He's running for the *governorship* again.
Her *governorship* lasted eight years.
Three *governorships* are up for election this fall.

gloss: An informal short word for a graduate of a school or college.
examples: Most recent *grads* leave with student debt.
He's a *grad* of Ohio State.
The firm hires about fifty *grads* a year.
contrast: Short for graduate; in grad school it means graduate-level study (аспирантура).

gloss: A student in a particular school grade, or a person who scores tests and papers.
examples: My son is a fourth *grader*.
The *graders* took two weeks to finish the exams.
Third *graders* start learning cursive at this school.

gloss: The work of giving marks or scores to students' work.
examples: *Grading* takes up most of her Sundays.
The professor explained his *grading* policy on the first day.
*Grading* on a curve is common in large lecture classes.

gloss: Something eagerly searched for, named after the legendary cup of the Arthurian stories.
examples: A cheap, safe battery is the holy *grail* of the industry.
For collectors, that record is the *grail*.
Fusion power is one of the great *grails* of science.

gloss: A chess player who holds the highest international title.
examples: She became a *grandmaster* at fifteen.
Two *grandmasters* played to a draw.
The tournament drew a dozen *grandmasters*.

gloss: The main seating structure for spectators at a stadium or racetrack.
examples: We sat in the *grandstand* near the finish line.
The *grandstand* was packed for the final.
Rain drove everyone under the *grandstands*.

gloss: An informal, affectionate word for a grandmother.
examples: My *granny* lives in Florida now.
He learned the recipe from his *granny*.
The park was full of *grannies* pushing strollers.

gloss: A picture, chart, or drawing used to present information in print or on a screen.
examples: The article includes a *graphic* showing the tax changes.
The game's *graphics* are stunning.
She designs *graphics* for a news website.

gloss: A large open area covered mainly with grass rather than trees.
examples: Bison once roamed these *grasslands*.
The park protects a stretch of native *grassland*.
Much of the state's *grassland* has been plowed under.

gloss: The natural force that pulls objects with mass toward each other.
examples: Newton's law of *gravitation* explains the orbits of the planets.
*Gravitation* holds the solar system together.
The tides are caused by the *gravitation* of the moon.

gloss: The quality of being remarkably important, talented, or admirable.
examples: The coach saw *greatness* in her from the start.
Nobody disputes his *greatness* as a writer.
The book asks what *greatness* really means.

gloss: An employee whose job is to welcome customers at the door.
examples: A *greeter* handed us a cart on the way in.
She works as a *greeter* at the front of the store.
The restaurant hired two more *greeters* for the holidays.

gloss: A flat metal cooking surface used for pancakes, eggs, and burgers.
examples: He poured the batter onto the hot *griddle*.
The diner has a *griddle* right behind the counter.
Most electric *griddles* are easy to clean.

gloss: A complaint about unfair treatment, especially one made formally.
examples: The union filed a *grievance* over the schedule.
He listed his *grievances* one by one.
She has a legitimate *grievance* against the company.

gloss: A twisted expression of the face showing pain or dislike.
examples: He answered with a *grimace*.
A *grimace* crossed her face when she stood up.
The photos caught a whole series of *grimaces*.

gloss: Long, dull, exhausting work or routine.
examples: The daily *grind* wears you down.
Studying for the bar exam was a real *grind*.
After two years of that *grind*, she quit.

gloss: A rotating stone wheel used for sharpening tools.
examples: He sharpened the ax on the *grindstone*.
Keep your nose to the *grindstone* and you'll be done by Friday.
The old mill still has two *grindstones*.

ru: гринго (иностранец, особ. американец, в Латинской Америке)
gloss: A foreigner in Latin America, especially an American, often said mockingly.
examples: The vendors could spot a *gringo* a mile away.
He was the only *gringo* on the bus.
Prices go up as soon as the *gringos* show up.

gloss: A firm hold on something, or the part of an object that you hold.
examples: He tightened his *grip* on the railing.
The bat has a new rubber *grip*.
She lost her *grip* and dropped the box.

gloss: A small, often repeated complaint.
examples: My only *gripe* is the price.
He had a few *gripes* about the hotel.
That's a common *gripe* among drivers here.

gloss: Coarsely ground corn boiled into a thick porridge, popular in the American South.
examples: He ordered eggs, bacon, and *grits*.
*Grits* taste better with butter and salt.
Nobody makes *grits* like my grandmother.
contrast: Used only in this plural form — there is no singular a grit for the food.

gloss: A large brown bear of western North America.
examples: A *grizzly* was spotted near the campground.
*Grizzlies* fish for salmon in the fall.
Hikers carry bear spray because of the *grizzlies*.
contrast: Don't confuse it with grisly (жуткий), which sounds almost the same.

gloss: A long, low sound made in pain, annoyance, or disappointment.
examples: He let out a *groan* and rolled over.
The joke got *groans* from the whole room.
A *groan* went up when the flight was canceled.
contrast: Sounds exactly like grown, the past participle of grow.

gloss: A person or business that sells food and household supplies.
examples: The corner *grocer* stays open until midnight.
Online *grocers* deliver the same day now.
She has worked for the same *grocer* for years.

gloss: A store that sells food, or, in the plural, the food someone buys there.
examples: Can you help me carry the *groceries*?
We stopped at the *grocery* on the way home.
*Groceries* cost noticeably more than last year.
contrast: In the plural, groceries means the food itself (продукты), not the stores.

gloss: A small cave, or an artificial one built as a decorative feature.
examples: The trail ends at a cool, dark *grotto*.
There's a *grotto* behind the waterfall.
The garden had statues and two little *grottoes*.

gloss: A bad-tempered person who complains a lot.
examples: Don't mind him, he's just an old *grouch*.
I turn into a *grouch* without coffee.
Every office has its *grouches*.

gloss: The basic preparation that makes later work possible.
examples: The meeting laid the *groundwork* for a deal.
Years of *groundwork* went into the study.
Somebody has to do the *groundwork* first.

gloss: A number of people or things gathered together or classed together.
examples: A *group* of tourists blocked the sidewalk.
We were split into *groups* of four.
She sings in a *group* on weekends.

gloss: A devoted fan who follows a band or celebrity from place to place.
examples: *Groupies* waited outside the tour bus.
He wrote a song about a *groupie*.
She jokes that she's a *groupie* for the local team.

gloss: The tendency of a group to agree with itself and stop questioning its own decisions.
examples: The report blamed *groupthink* for the failure.
Bringing in outsiders helps prevent *groupthink*.
*Groupthink* is a real danger on small teams.

gloss: A thin, watery porridge made by boiling grain in water or milk.
examples: The orphans were fed *gruel* twice a day.
He served us something like cold *gruel*.
*Gruel* was standard food in the workhouse.

gloss: A quiet complaint muttered to yourself or to other people.
examples: There were *grumbles* about the new parking rules.
He agreed with a *grumble*.
The change went through with only a few *grumbles*.

gloss: A short, low sound made in the throat, like the noise a pig makes.
examples: He answered with a *grunt*.
You could hear *grunts* coming from the weight room.
The pig gave a satisfied *grunt*.

gloss: A Mexican dip made from mashed avocado, lime, and seasonings.
examples: The chips came with *guacamole*.
She makes *guacamole* with a lot of cilantro.
Extra *guacamole* costs two dollars.

gloss: A person or institution that promises to pay someone else's debt if that person cannot.
examples: Her father signed the lease as a *guarantor*.
The bank required a *guarantor* for the loan.
*Guarantors* are liable for the full amount.

gloss: A loud, hearty burst of laughter.
examples: The line got a *guffaw* from the back row.
He let out a *guffaw* and slapped the table.
*Guffaws* filled the little theater.

gloss: Advice or direction given by someone with more knowledge or authority.
examples: She offered some *guidance* on choosing classes.
The agency issued new *guidance* for schools.
Under his *guidance*, the team improved quickly.

gloss: An outward appearance or pretense that hides what something really is.
examples: The fee was raised under the *guise* of a service charge.
He came back in the *guise* of a reformer.
The same idea shows up in different *guises*.
contrast: Sounds exactly like guys (ребята); only the spelling differs.

gloss: A thick Louisiana stew of meat or seafood, vegetables, and rice.
examples: She made a pot of shrimp *gumbo*.
The *gumbo* at that place is worth the drive.
Good *gumbo* starts with a dark roux.

gloss: A small, chewy, sugar-coated candy made with gelatin.
examples: The gingerbread house was covered in *gumdrops*.
He picked the green *gumdrop* out of the bowl.
*Gumdrops* stick to your teeth.

gloss: A fight in which people shoot at each other with guns.
examples: Two officers were injured in the *gunfight*.
The movie ends with a *gunfight* in the street.
*Gunfights* between the gangs went on for weeks.

gloss: A man who uses a gun to attack or threaten people.
examples: A *gunman* opened fire outside the courthouse.
Police arrested the *gunman* an hour later.
Two *gunmen* fled in a black sedan.

gloss: A person who makes or repairs guns.
examples: He took the rifle to a *gunsmith*.
The shop employs two *gunsmiths*.
Her grandfather was a *gunsmith* in Pennsylvania.

gloss: A respected teacher or expert whose advice people follow.
examples: He's a fitness *guru* with a million followers.
The company brought in a marketing *guru*.
Tech *gurus* have been predicting this for years.

gloss: Obvious enjoyment and energy in doing something.
examples: He attacked the sandwich with *gusto*.
She sang the last verse with real *gusto*.
They took up the project with great *gusto*.

gloss: An informal word for a man, or, in the plural, for a group of people of any gender.
examples: Some *guy* left his jacket here.
Are you *guys* ready to go?
He's a good *guy*.

gloss: Something or someone that uses up a lot, especially a vehicle that burns a lot of fuel.
examples: That truck is a real gas *guzzler*.
Old refrigerators are energy *guzzlers*.
High gas prices made *guzzlers* hard to sell.

gloss: A soft white mineral used to make plaster and drywall.
examples: The interior walls are *gypsum* board.
*Gypsum* is mined a few miles from here.
Farmers spread *gypsum* to loosen heavy soil.
contrast: The g sounds like j: JIP-suhm.

gloss: A spinning wheel mounted so that it holds its position, used to keep things steady or to sense direction.
examples: Your phone has a tiny *gyroscope* inside it.
The ship's *gyroscope* keeps the camera level.
He showed the class how a *gyroscope* stays upright.

gloss: A short Japanese poem of three lines and seventeen syllables.
examples: The class wrote a *haiku* about winter.
She posts a *haiku* every morning.
His book collects two hundred *haiku*.
contrast: The plural is usually haiku, unchanged, though haikus is also heard.

gloss: A storm in which balls of ice fall instead of rain.
examples: A *hailstorm* smashed the greenhouse.
The *hailstorm* dented every car on the lot.
Spring *hailstorms* are common in Texas.

gloss: A clever shortcut for doing something, or an illegal break-in to a computer system.
examples: Here's a *hack* for peeling garlic quickly.
The bank disclosed a *hack* that exposed customer data.
The site is full of cleaning *hacks*.
